posts.title: Indemnity periods and the kiln that takes 14 months
posts.excerpt: A standard twelve-month business interruption indemnity period often proves disastrously short when specialist commercial plant requires custom overseas manufacture and commissioning.
posts.content:
When commercial business owners arrange property insurance, the replacement value of physical buildings and equipment receives intense scrutiny. Yet the business interruption section of the schedule—the mechanism intended to replace lost income, sustain payroll, and cover ongoing debt service while premises are rebuilt—is frequently treated as a secondary consideration. In most standard policies, brokers simply insert a default twelve-month indemnity period without interrogating the operational realities of the client's manufacturing or processing operations. For many industrial firms, twelve months is not merely tight; it is a mathematical certainty of insolvency following a total loss.

The fundamental misunderstanding lies in what an indemnity period actually measures. Business owners often assume that twelve months refers to the time required to erect a replacement structure. But insurance indemnity does not end when the roof is sealed. It ends only when trading returns to the financial level the business would have achieved had no damage occurred. Between the day of a major fire and the resumption of normal turnover lies a sequence of unavoidable, compounding delays that cannot be rushed by goodwill or cash settlements.

Consider the real-world situation we encountered when conducting a cover review for a regional timber merchant operating two yards in Calder Bay. Their existing commercial package carried a business interruption indemnity period of just six months. During our ninety-minute site walk across the drying sheds and timber bays, our surveyor examined their primary industrial drying kiln. The kiln was an engineered, bespoke unit imported from a specialist manufacturer in northern Europe.

We sat down with the owner to map out a realistic reconstruction timeline. Clearing debris and contaminated ash from a timber yard fire requires environmental assessments and licensed disposal, easily consuming two months. Planning permits and structural sign-offs for an industrial facility take at least three months. From the placement of the purchase order, the European manufacturer required eight months to fabricate the bespoke drying kiln components, followed by shipping and two months on-site for mechanical installation, ductwork, and digital sensor calibration.

In total, restoring the kiln to full operational temperature and re-establishing seasoned lumber stock would take fourteen months under ideal conditions. Had the timber merchant suffered a total loss under their existing policy, their insurance payments for lost gross profit and continuing staff wages would have ceased after month six. The business would have faced eight full months of heavy operational expenditure with zero manufacturing output, an outcome that no medium-sized family firm can survive.

Extending an indemnity period from twelve to twenty-four or thirty-six months does not double or triple the premium. In commercial underwriting, the premium rate per thousand euros of cover decreases significantly as indemnity periods lengthen, because the probability of an interruption lasting into a second or third year is substantially lower than an interruption occurring in the first. The additional premium required to secure a twenty-four-month period is negligible compared to the catastrophic financial exposure of running out of cash halfway through a machinery rebuild.

Reading the policy wording alone will never uncover these operational vulnerabilities. An underwriter sitting behind a desk hundreds of miles away does not know that your drying kiln takes fourteen months to build, just as they do not know the lead times for your packaging lines or bespoke injection moulds. Uncovering the true recovery horizon requires standing on the workshop floor, inspecting the machinery, and asking direct questions about suppliers, shipping routes, and commissioning schedules before binding cover.
